overview: I2203 turns holding from a diagram exercise into an instrument task-management drill. The event standard is to enter protected airspace correctly, measure the no-wind orbit, apply drift and timing corrections, and keep the aircraft recoverable if an electrical failure strips the cockpit down to backup instruments and standby communication.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Holding entry begins before the fix: copy the clearance, determine the holding side and pattern direction, slow in time, and know the first outbound heading before crossing.

children.text: Start the speed reduction within 3 minutes or 5 NM of the holding fix when clearance beyond the fix has not been received.
The normal T-6B holding airspeed is 150 KIAS; published maximum holding speeds still matter for altitude and field-specific restrictions.
A standard pattern uses right turns; a non-standard pattern uses left turns. If turn direction is not stated, right turns are implied.
If timing is used, the inbound leg is normally 1 minute at or below 14,000 feet MSL and 1 1/2 minutes above 14,000 feet MSL.

For a standard pattern, parallel entry is used when the reciprocal of the holding course lies between the heading index and 110 degrees left; teardrop is between the heading index and 70 degrees right; otherwise use direct entry.
For a non-standard pattern, mirror the logic: parallel is to the right, teardrop is to the left, and direct is the remaining sector.
Standard teardrop heading is 30 degrees less than the reciprocal of the holding course; non-standard teardrop heading is 30 degrees more.
If the reciprocal is within 5 degrees of an entry boundary, either entry is acceptable.
Use the six Ts to keep task order clean: time, turn, time, transition, twist, talk.
Report established in holding with position, time, and altitude when required; confirm EFC at least 5 minutes prior if needed.
At the end of the outbound leg, turn inbound toward the holding radial using tail-radial-turn and intercept the holding course promptly.

items.text: The no-wind orbit begins on the second passage of the holding fix and gives you the information needed to correct both heading and timing.

children.text: Cross the fix, reset elapsed time, and turn in the pattern direction to the no-wind outbound heading, which is the reciprocal of the holding course.
Start outbound timing when wings level or abeam the holding fix, whichever occurs last.
If abeam cannot be determined, start timing when wings level.
At the end of the outbound leg, turn inbound toward the holding radial and start inbound timing when wings level on course or with an appropriate intercept established.
An on-course inbound rollout suggests no crosswind component.
An undershoot suggests crosswind from the non-holding side.
An overshoot suggests crosswind from the holding side.
Once established inbound, use normal tracking procedures to find the wind-corrected heading and note the crab angle.
Note inbound time at the fix if timing corrections are required for the next orbit.
Keep basic airwork clean; altitude, heading, and airspeed errors contaminate the wind picture you are trying to measure.

items.text: Holding corrections apply the no-wind orbit lesson: correct outbound heading for drift, adjust outbound time for inbound timing, then refine on each orbit.

children.text: Triple the inbound drift correction for the outbound leg; for example, an 8-degree right crab inbound becomes a 24-degree left correction outbound.
Hold triple drift for no more than 1 minute outbound.
If the outbound leg continues beyond 1 minute, transition to single drift for the remaining time.
If no-wind inbound time exceeded 90 seconds, the first wind-corrected outbound time should be no less than 30 seconds.
Adjust outbound time to fix the previous inbound time. If inbound was 10 seconds short, add 10 seconds outbound; if inbound was long, subtract time.
Subsequent orbits are fine-tuning passes, not proof that the first correction was bad.
Inbound legs are tracked on the holding course; outbound legs are flown as headings.
Keep fuel and EFC time in the scan, especially in stacked holding where vertical separation can be as little as 1000 feet.

Common errors are using the drift correction in the wrong direction, forgetting to transition from triple drift to single drift, trying to track outbound, and letting basic airwork or magnetic-variation confusion drive false corrections.

items.text: Battery and generator failure assumes the generator has failed and the main battery is depleted. In IMC, the problem is maintaining control with a stripped cockpit while getting below oxygen and pressurization risk.

children.text: Only auxiliary-battery-powered essentials remain: backup flight instrument, FIRE 1 detection, IRU, and VHF radio through the standby VHF control head.

Major losses include OBOGS, ICS, all electronic displays, PMU, starter, FIRE 2, landing-gear indicators, normal flap operation and indications, probes anti-ice, interior/exterior lighting, ECS/pressurization, UHF, GPS, VHF NAV, DME, transponder, and TCAS.
OBOGS is inoperative once the main battery is depleted or with battery failure, and the cockpit will depressurize when power to the battery bus is lost.
Initiate descent below 10,000 feet MSL as required.
Turn AUX BAT ON to power the backup flight instrument and standby VHF path for about 30 minutes.
Plan to extend the landing gear with the emergency extension system; emergency flaps will not be available if the main battery has failed, and flaps may retract if battery-bus power is lost.
Land as soon as possible.
In an instrument event, immediately transition your scan to the BFI, preserve attitude and airspeed, and use standby VHF/ATC help before task-saturating on lost displays.
A PAR or ASR/no-gyro recovery may be feasible if conditions, communication, and remaining instruments support it; brief it as a recovery option, not a guarantee.

studyNotes.summary: Enter holding deliberately, use the no-wind orbit to measure wind, correct with triple drift and timing, and keep the BFI/standby-VHF recovery plan ready for battery and generator failure.
